children.text: At about

above sea level, this is Cavite's highest mountain. Climb the forest trail to the summit and a massive rock peak jutting up like a parrot's beak, the western sea, and Manila Bay all come into view at once, making it a top pick for a day hike near Manila.
Mount Pico de Loro rises about

above sea level at the border of Ternate and Maragondon in Cavite Province and Nasugbu in Batangas Province, making it Cavite's highest peak. Its name, Spanish for "parrot's beak," comes from the massive rock outcrop (a monolith) jutting out beside the summit like a beak. Formed by ancient volcanic activity, this rock is such a distinct landmark that it can be seen from ships passing far off in Manila Bay, and it has long served as a marker for sailors.

The mountain lies within the Mts. Palay-Palay–Mataas-na-Gulod Protected Landscape, managed by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR). It's one of the few remaining lowland forests in southwestern Luzon, home to Philippine endemic birds, monkeys, and a variety of butterflies. What makes this mountain special is that most of the trail runs beneath dense forest shade before suddenly opening up near the summit to reveal the South China Sea (West Philippine Sea), the Nasugbu coast, and the waters toward Corregidor Island.

At one time, hundreds of people flocked here every weekend, causing serious litter and damage, so the mountain went through several closures and rehabilitations. It now operates under an online advance-booking system, a daily visitor cap, and mandatory guides. Climbing to the top of the monolith by rope, as people once did, is now banned for safety reasons, so the hike has shifted to admiring the rock peak from the summit and viewpoints instead.

It suits beginner-to-intermediate hikers with some experience, expat hiking clubs looking for a proper mountain they can do as a day trip from Manila, and travelers who love mountain scenery with sea views. Even those with limited stamina can manage it by climbing slowly, but with the midday heat and steep sections, it's not a casual stroll.
The protected area was first designated a national park and bird sanctuary on
October 26, 1976
, and became a protected landscape under Presidential Proclamation No. 1315 in

. Covering about 3,973 hectares across Ternate and Maragondon in Cavite and Nasugbu in Batangas, it is the last remaining lowland rainforest in Cavite Province and an important water source for the province. As for the mountain's height, hikers have long used
, but the protected area management office and Wikipedia list it as
, so figures vary by source. The same range continues with Mataas na Gulod (
), Mount Marami, Mount Nagpatong, and others, and it was around Mount Nagpatong in this very range that revolutionary leader Andres Bonifacio was executed in

blocks.title: View the parrot's-beak rock from the summit

children.text: Standing at the summit, the massive rock peak rises right beside you with the sea spreading out behind it. It's the mountain's signature view, and on a clear day the coastlines of Batangas and Cavite appear to stretch on together.

From the jump-off point to the summit, you walk mostly under tree shade. You'll cross streams and pass through bamboo groves and rocky sections, enjoying the forest's changing character along the way.

blocks.title: Early-morning sea of clouds and sunlight

children.text: Set off before dawn in the dry season and you'll find a thin mist settled in the valley below, with the rock at the summit lit by soft morning light.

As befits a protected area, you may come across Philippine endemic birds and monkeys. Walk quietly and listen to the sounds of the forest. The management office's materials feature birds such as the Luzon hornbill, Philippine trogon, and Philippine eagle-owl, and troops of Philippine long-tailed macaques also live in the forest around the station.
From the summit viewpoint you can frame the rock peak and the sea in a single shot. A wide-angle lens or your phone's wide mode comes in handy.
Come down from the mountain and cool off at a beach in Nasugbu or Ternate, about
30–40 minutes
away by car, for the perfect day.
On the way back, stop by Maragondon town, home to an 18th-century church and the house where revolutionary leader Andres Bonifacio was tried.
The trail runs about
3.5km
one way from the station to the summit. It starts on a flat path beside a stream and passes through tall forest and stair sections; after about
1 hour 30 minutes
you reach a view deck where the sea opens up, and about
30 minutes
more of climbing brings you to the old campsite and the final steep pitch below the summit. When the trail reopened in
, stairs were installed near the summit, making the climb much easier even for beginners.

, so don't leave it too late. After the descent it can be hard to find a tricycle in front of the station, so arrange a pickup time with the driver who took you up in the morning. The Bonifacio Trial House is usually closed on Mondays and Sundays but open on Fridays and Saturdays, the hiking days (check opening hours before you go).

From Manila, take Coastal Road (CAVITEX) south into Cavite, then follow Antero Soriano Highway to Ternate. Drive through Ternate town and up the mountain road toward Nasugbu (toward Kaybiang Tunnel), and you'll reach the DENR jump-off point. It's about
and takes
2–2.5 hours
in the early morning. There's parking around the jump-off, and a parking fee is charged.

The main jump-off is the DENR station near Magnetic Hill on the Ternate–Nasugbu road. Set your navigation to "Pico de Loro DENR Station" or Magnetic Hill. There are almost no lights on the road before dawn and it is easy to drive past the entrance, so slow down.
The station's official address is DENR Park Station, Sitio Malauyas, Brgy. Sapang I, Ternate. On arrival you watch a
15-minute
orientation video and sign a waiver before setting off; if you arrive late, you'll be pushed to the next time slot or set off last. Parking and guide fees are paid separately on site.
At PITX (the integrated bus terminal) in Parañaque, board a Ternate-bound bus such as Saulog Transit or Saint Anthony of Padua. The first bus leaves around
4 AM
; the ride takes about
2–3 hours
and costs about
one way. In Ternate town, hire a tricycle for the ride up to the DENR jump-off, which takes
20–30 minutes
; drivers often charge about
per person, so agree on a round-trip fare before you get on. Tricycles can be scarce before dawn, so it's best to arrange one with a driver the day before.
For clubs or groups, a chartered van from Manila is most convenient. For a 12-seater, it's about
per day (check whether fuel and tolls are extra).
If you're going solo or find booking and transportation a hassle, a joiner tour from Manila is convenient. At about
per person (based on a group of 4 or more), it includes round-trip air-conditioned transport, a guide, entrance fees, and permits; tours usually leave Manila at
and return around
. Check whether the tour company handles the official website booking for you, and whether it departs on Friday or Saturday.
From the Nasugbu side in Batangas, head north on the Ternate–Nasugbu road (N407). Completed in
, this coastal mountain road runs about
30km
and passes through the
Kaybiang Tunnel in the Maragondon section. It takes about
40–50 minutes
by car from Nasugbu town to the station, and about
1 hour 30 minutes
from Tagaytay via Nasugbu. The mountain stretch is a series of winding climbs and descents with almost no streetlights, so avoid driving at night.
The best time is the dry season,
November–April
December–February
morning temperatures drop into the low 20s (°C), making for pleasant hiking with long-range visibility.
March–April
has clear weather but very strong midday sun, so the exposed sections near the summit take a heavy toll on your energy. During this period it's best to set off at
5–6 AM
and come down before noon.
From late
May
through
October

is the wet season, when the trail turns to slippery mud and leeches can appear in the forest. When a typhoon or heavy rain warning is in effect, the protected area's management suspends all hiking. The protected area is also temporarily closed at times for scheduled rest-and-restoration periods or during high wildfire risk, so always check for notices before you set off.
Weekend and public holiday bookings often fill up 2–3 weeks in advance. If you have a specific date in mind, apply as soon as the booking window opens.
Weather data show that the area is hottest in
April
, with average midday temperatures of about
, while
July–September
is very wet, with monthly rainfall reaching 400–500mm. Hikes run only on Fridays and Saturdays, and bookings are accepted only from
30 days
to
2 days
before your visit, so time your application for one month before the date you want. After heavy rain, the whole mountain is sometimes closed for weeks for trail repairs. In fact, from
August 21–September 12, 2026
, all hiking in the protected area was suspended to repair damage from a typhoon and the southwest monsoon.

Most people do this as a day hike, but if an early-morning departure isn't appealing, you can stay the night before at a resort on the Ternate or Nasugbu coast. Resorts on the Ternate coast and beach lodgings toward Nasugbu run about
a night, about
20–40 minutes
from the jump-off by car. For an upscale resort, consider the resort cluster on the Nasugbu coast.

There's no shop on the mountain, so bring trail snacks and a packed lunch. After the descent, enjoy grilled fish, shrimp, and sinigang at a Filipino seafood restaurant on the Ternate or Nasugbu coast, or try pancit pusit (squid-ink noodles), a specialty of Cavite City. If you head back via Tagaytay, bulalo and buko pie at the highland restaurant row are also good choices.

Pico de Loro Cove, on the Nasugbu coast southwest of the mountain, shares the name and is easy to confuse, but it is a members-only resort complex within Hamilo Coast, developed by the SM group. Only members, guests invited by members, and guests of the Pico Sands Hotel inside the complex can enter, and it is not a trailhead, so set your navigation to the DENR station instead of this name. If you'd like to unwind at a beach resort the day before your hike, booking this hotel is one option.
You must book an official online reservation before hiking. Without a confirmation and ID on hand, you may be denied entry on site.
There are set operating days, a daily visitor cap, and a cutoff time for entering the trail. Check the protected area management office's official notice again the day before you set off.
Bring at least 2–3 liters of water per person. Unlike in the past, when there used to be a place selling water partway up, you can't count on resupply now.
Wear trekking shoes or running shoes with good grip. The trail mixes rocky sections and dirt paths, so sandals or everyday shoes are dangerous.
Gloves are handy for gripping ropes and rocks. Trekking poles greatly reduce the strain on your knees during the descent.
There's no shade near the summit, so a hat, sunscreen, and long-sleeve arm sleeves come in handy.
Mobile signal is unstable on the mountain, so don't get separated from your group, and save your guide's contact number.
The rule is to carry all your trash back out. Bring a small trash bag in your backpack.
The trail closed for rehabilitation in
October 2016
and reopened on
January 12, 2023
. Since then, the rules have been online booking through the Protected Area Management Board (PAMB), an entrance fee of
per person, a maximum of 5 hikers per guide, bringing ID, and no camping. New stairs have been installed near the summit for beginners.
On the
official booking site
you can choose only Friday or Saturday dates. If you don't pay the entrance fee through Landbank Link.BizPortal (DENR PENRO Cavite, under Visitor Fee) within
48 hours
of booking, your reservation is automatically canceled, and booking details such as names can be changed only by email up to
3 days
before your visit. Guide and parking fees are paid separately on site, so bring cash.
Climbing the parrot's-beak rock (the monolith) is prohibited. Falls have occurred in this section in the past, so never cross the warning line.
Don't stray from the designated trail. Camping, lighting fires, and collecting plants or animals within the protected area are violations that can be penalized.
The risk of heatstroke is high at midday. If you feel dizzy or get a headache, rest in the shade immediately and replenish fluids and electrolytes.
During the wet season, the muddy slopes are very slippery and leeches appear. Bring long socks and anti-leech spray.
If you push your schedule and descend late in the afternoon, the forest darkens quickly. Bring a headlamp and stick to the turnaround time your guide sets.
Illegally hiking in via a bypass route without a reservation is subject to enforcement, and rescue is difficult if an accident occurs.

Hikers under 17 are not allowed, and you may not bring in pets, alcohol, speakers or musical instruments, or dangerous items; smoking is also prohibited. If even one member of your group is under the influence of alcohol or drugs or breaks the prohibited-items rules, the entire group will be refused entry.
